title: Normal approximation and continuity correction
section: Probability and Statistics ▷ The Normal Approximation to the Binomial Distribution
terms: normal approximation to binomial; continuity correction; binomial standard deviation; approximation regime.

exposition.text:
For X ∼ Bin(n, p), a normal approximation uses mean np and variance np(1 − p). It is useful
when both expected successes and failures are reasonably large; extreme tails or very small p
may require greater care or a different approximation. The result is approximate, not an exact
equality.
Continuity correction matches each integer mass to a unit interval. Thus P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is
q
approximated by Φ((b + 1/2 − np)/σ) − Φ((a − 1/2 − np)/σ) with σ = np(1 − p). For P(X ≥ k)
the corrected boundary is k − 1/2, while P (X > k) uses k + 1/2.
For a sequence of binomial models, a normal limit for the standardized count holds when both

conservative design rule. This is an approximation-based calculation, not an exact finite-sample
probability guarantee.

question.text:
For X ∼ Bin(100, 1/2), which is the continuity-corrected normal approximation to P (X ≥ 60)?
(A) 1 − Φ(2.1) (B) 1 − Φ(2) (C) 1 − Φ(1.9) (D) Φ(1.9) (E) Φ(2.1) − Φ(1.9)

solution.text:
The mean is 50 and standard deviation 5. The event X ≥ 60 begins at corrected boundary
59.5, so the standardized threshold is (59.5 − 50)/5 = 1.9.

The integer event is 90 ≤ X ≤ 109, so use the continuous interval [89.5, 109.5]. The mean
is 100 and variance 400(1/4)(3/4) = 75, yielding upper and lower standardized endpoints

two-sided margin 0.01 at cutoff z = 1.96. With the true proportion unknown, use the conserva-

prescribe?
